g_open: Three of us put our shoulders to that door. Big men. It did not give an inch. ... And there was nothing on the other side but an empty room.
g_s1: Renvyle. The end of Europe — Connemara, the house standing between the mountains and the Atlantic. I bought it for the peace. [soft laugh] A surgeon buys a house for peace... and finds his servants will not sleep in it. Footsteps, in the empty upstairs. Candles quenched. Not blown out — quenched. The way you'd pinch a wick.
g_s2: There was one room the disturbances favoured. And one night, its door would not open. I put my shoulder to it. Then two others joined me. [exhales] Three grown men, against one unlocked door — and it stood like masonry. ... And then it gave. All at once. Onto an empty room. And a window shut fast.
g_s3: My guest was Willie Yeats. The poet. Nothing in this world or the next could frighten that man — he was delighted, of course. [soft laugh] His wife had the gift, or something very like it. So they sat a vigil, in that room. [pause] And she saw him come through. A boy. Fourteen, perhaps. Pale, with great... luminous eyes. A child of the Blakes — who had held that house three hundred years before us.
g_s4: He objected to us. Strangers, in his house. He was a Blake; we were interlopers. [exhales] He asked — through her — for incense. And flowers. ... The oldest rents in the world. And we paid them.
g_s5: In twenty-three, in the Troubles, they burned Renvyle to the ground. I wrote at the time: Renvyle House, with its irreplaceable oak panelling, is burned down. They say it took a week to burn. [pause] We rebuilt it, as an hotel. People stay there still. ... And if footsteps cross the empty upstairs at night — well. [exhales] It is his house too. It always was.
